title: Praise, then ask
hook: the Fatiha praises for four verses before it asks for anything (1:1–7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: a conversation, and your line, he answers each line. Today, look at the order those lines come in.

A text arrives: can you lend me fifty dollars. No hello. No how are you. Just the ask. Nothing wrong with it, exactly, but it lands hard. Now a different text: I was thinking about you this morning, you were so good to me last month, and, I hate to ask, could you help me out. Same request. Different weight. The Fatiha is seven verses long, and for the first four of them it asks for nothing at all. Today: praise.
screen: `JUST THE ASK.` → `OR: HELLO, THANK YOU, THEN THE ASK.` → `FOUR VERSES BEFORE ANY REQUEST.`

segments.voice: Count the verses as day three hundred thirty-three did, with the bismillah first. One: in the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful. Two: praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds. Three: the Beneficent, the Merciful. Four: Owner of the Day of Judgment. Four verses, every one of them about who God is. Then verse five turns: Thee alone we worship, Thee alone we ask for help. Only in verses six and seven comes a request: show us the straight path. A hadith makes that order explicit. Fadalah ibn Ubayd reported, in the collections of Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ heard a man making a supplication in his prayer without praising God or sending blessings on the Prophet. He said: this man has rushed. Then he taught: when one of you prays, begin with the praise of your Lord, then send blessings on the Prophet, then ask for whatever you wish. So Muslim supplications are often taught in that shape: praise, blessing, then the need. Praise puts the one being addressed first, before the want. It also changes the asking. A request made after four verses about mercy, lordship and judgment comes out smaller and clearer. The straight path, in the Fatiha, isn't a demand. It's what you ask for after you've remembered whom you're asking.
screen: `FOUR VERSES ABOUT WHO GOD IS` · `VERSE FIVE: THE TURN` · `THIS MAN HAS RUSHED` · `PRAISE, BLESSING, THEN THE NEED`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you want, something real, large or small, and hold it without saying it yet. First, for a few breaths, name what you're grateful for, or, if you pray, what you know of God: merciful, near, the Lord of the worlds. Then let the request come, and hear whether it sounds different when it finally arrives.
Praise. The Fatiha spends four verses on who God is before it asks for anything, and the hadith calls skipping that step rushing. Today's word.
Your line: praise first. The asking can wait four verses. That's day three hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Many Muslims open a du'a by praising Allah and sending blessings on the Prophet before making their request, following the order of al-Fatiha and the hadith of Fadalah ibn Ubayd.

fork.setup: a man in the mosque prays, and goes straight to what he needs. the Prophet hears him. what does he say?
options: this man's prayer is not accepted.
nothing; a request is a request.
fork.reveal: he rushed. the Prophet doesn't reject the prayer; he teaches the order: praise, blessing on the Prophet, then ask for whatever you wish.

original.note: Arabic: extolling, speaking well of someone; often used for the praise that opens a du'a.

chat.says: Why does the Fatiha wait four verses before asking God for anything?
options: It praises first; a hadith calls asking without praise rushing.
It doesn't ask; the Fatiha is only praise, with no request.
The first verses are for the imam; the request is for everyone.
chat.meaning: The Prophet heard a man ask without praise and said: this man has rushed. Begin with praise, then blessings, then ask.

bismillah.meaning: in the name of Allah; counted here as verse one

notes: Hadith of Fadalah ibn Ubayd: numbers (Abu Dawud 1481, Tirmidhi 3477) and wording ('he has rushed') cited from memory; please confirm. At-Tirmidhi grades it hasan sahih in common editions; confirm.
Four verses of praise assumes the count with the bismillah as verse one, matching the index and day 333.
Pickthall's 'Owner of the Day of Judgment' is quoted as it appears in year one; the other verses are paraphrased.
